soil-water-188.title: Two rings to keep the flow straight down
soil-water-188.text: One ring of water guards another. A double-ring infiltrometer sets a larger outer ring around an inner one, and the outer ring keeps the flow from the inner ring one-dimensional. Water is supplied at constant or falling head. The operator records how much enters the soil from the inner ring over a set time. With steady one-dimensional flow and a unit gradient below, the infiltration rate approximately equals the saturated hydraulic conductivity. The ASTM standard method uses inner and outer rings of 30 and 60 cm diameter.

soil-water-170.title: Counting slowed neutrons to find hidden water
soil-water-170.text: Hydrogen gives water away. In a neutron probe, a pellet of americium-241 and beryllium produces fast neutrons when alpha particles from the americium strike the beryllium nuclei. They slow down when they hit hydrogen nuclei in the soil. Counting the slow neutrons that return estimates the hydrogen present, and so the water. Read through an access tube installed in the soil, the probe gives farmers highly accurate deep-soil readings. Neutron probes can gauge soil water potential over a range of 0 to −1500 kPa.

soil-water-207.title: The root zone, the soil that plants can reach
soil-water-207.text: Water that sinks below the roots is water a plant will never use. The soil moisture zone, often called the root zone, is the depth of soil from which plant roots draw water. Water that moves below it after heavy rain or irrigation is lost to plants, and it can take fertilizers and nutrients with it. Good {{ref:soil-water-234}} therefore aims to wet the whole root zone while keeping overwatering to a minimum. Salts that build up in the root zone can be carried deeper, or into groundwater, by {{ref:soil-water-210}}.

soil-water-226.title: Sensing soil moisture through a circuit's frequency
soil-water-226.text: Wet soil changes the rhythm of an electronic circuit. A frequency domain sensor measures soil moisture with an oscillating circuit whose operating frequency depends on the dielectric constant of the soil around it. Its two types are capacitance probes and electrical impedance sensors. Impedance sensors commonly feed a 100 MHz oscillator signal along a coaxial line into buried probe wires, then measure the part reflected where impedance changes. These sensors are cheaper to build and respond faster than TDR. But the complex field around the probe means calibrating for each kind of soil, unless a high frequency is used.

soil-water-157.title: Shortcuts: how water races down root and worm channels
soil-water-157.text: Tree roots, living or dead, can raise infiltration rates up to 27 times. They do it by opening channels for rainwater. Preferential flow is the rapid drainage of water under gravity along connected macropores, crevices, and root and worm channels. Instead of soaking evenly through the soil, the water takes the express route. Macropores and fractures strongly influence infiltration rates, flow patterns and hydraulic conductivity in many soils. Soil mixing by organisms and other disturbances opens paths for gas in the soil as well as water. Even strongly water-repellent patches play a part, because water that cannot enter them finds pathways deeper into the profile. The shortcuts have costs. They speed drainage, but they also carry dissolved nutrients away quickly and leave water and chemicals unevenly spread. Extreme forms in depressions speed contaminants toward groundwater. They also distort measurement. In soils with distinct macropores, preferential flow dominates readings from single- or double-ring infiltrometers under ponding. Soil physics models often add it as dual-porosity or dual-permeability options. These are generally bolted onto solutions of the {{ref:soil-water-238}} without rigorous physical grounding.

soil-water-210.title: Groundwater recharge: how rain refills aquifers
soil-water-210.text: Most of the water in an aquifer arrived from above. Groundwater recharge, also called deep drainage, is the downward movement of water from the surface to groundwater, and it is the main way water enters an aquifer. Rain and snowmelt feed it mainly, rivers and lakes less. It usually takes place in unsaturated ground below plant roots and is often expressed as a flux to the water table. Diffuse recharge is rain soaking through soil over large areas. Focused recharge leaks from rivers, lakes, wetlands or depressions, and it grows more dominant as climates get drier. People push the balance both ways. Paving, development and logging can strip topsoil, reduce infiltration, increase runoff and so cut recharge. Yet urban recharge can be up to ten times higher than rural, because leaking water-supply and sewage networks add water that rural areas lack. Recharge can also flush salts that accumulate in the root zone into deeper layers or into groundwater. For sustainable use, long-term pumping from an aquifer should not exceed its recharge. Climate change may cut both ways too. Fewer but more intense storms may raise recharge in many places, while harsher droughts may dry and compact soils and reduce infiltration.

soil-water-212.title: Refilling aquifers on purpose
soil-water-212.text: In Orange County, California, one facility cleans and injects 100 million gallons of water a day, or 90 billion gallons a year. That is artificial groundwater recharge: recharge engineered by people, routing rainwater or reclaimed water into the subsurface. Managed aquifer recharge methods include modifying streambed channels, bank filtration, water spreading and recharge wells. In India, farmers' over-pumping has depleted groundwater. In 2007 the government funded dug-well recharge projects in 100 districts of seven states. Cities face a related task. Stormwater pollution collects in retention basins, and high water tables affect how detention ponds, retention ponds and rain gardens should be designed.

soil-water-177.title: Field capacity: the water a soil keeps after draining
soil-water-177.text: Two to three days after rain, a well-drained soil settles down. Field capacity is the water a soil still holds after excess water has drained away and downward movement has slowed. By convention it is the water content held at −33 kPa of suction, or −10 kPa for sandy soils, after work by Richards and Weaver. At this point the smallest pores hold water and the largest hold air, the best condition for plant growth and microbial activity. The water held depends on the particles' specific surface area, so clay-rich and organic soils have higher field capacities. It is measured by wetting a profile, covering it against evaporation and tracking water content. The term came from Israelsen and West and from Veihmeyer and Hendrickson, improving on Lyman Briggs's {{ref:soil-water-245}}. Veihmeyer and Hendrickson admitted it is not strictly a constant, but a practical measure of water-holding capacity. When more water reaches a soil than its field capacity, groundwater recharge is most likely.

soil-water-229.title: Available water: the share of soil water plants can use
soil-water-229.text: Not all the water in a soil is water a plant can use. Available water capacity is the amount a soil profile can store and make available to growing crops. It is also called available water content (AWC), profile available water (PAW) or total available water (TAW). Frank Veihmeyer and Arthur Hendrickson defined readily available water as the difference between the water content at field capacity and at the permanent wilting point. This water sits in pores of 0.1–75 μm. Smaller cryptopores hold water too tightly for roots, and macropores are generally air-filled at field capacity. The definition is disputed. Daniel Hillel argued that its two limits were never clearly defined and lack a physical basis. Water, he said, is never equally available across the range. Richards, profiled in {{ref:soil-hist-023}}, called it oversimplified, since availability also depends on how readily soil water moves in to replace what roots take. Strongly alkaline, sodium-rich soils hold little, as do thin soils of the kind in {{ref:soil-class-050}}, while sepiolite clay can raise plant-available water in sandy soils.

soil-water-234.title: Deciding when to water, and for how long
soil-water-234.text: Up to 50% of landscape water is wasted by inefficient methods, the EPA WaterSense program estimates. Irrigation scheduling is how managers decide how often and for how long to water. The aim is to wet the whole root zone while minimizing overwatering and keeping water use efficiency high. Refilling depleted water before stress sets in avoids moisture stress. Methods range from watching plants for wilting and judging soil by feel, through sensors in the root zone, to {{ref:soil-water-235}}. Root-zone sensors include capacitance sensors, neutron probes for accurate deep readings, and the {{ref:soil-water-221}}. Scheduling has moved from calendar timers to smart controllers that respond to weather-based evapotranspiration or to measured soil moisture. Soil-based controllers either skip a timed cycle when the soil is wet or start watering only when moisture falls to a set threshold. Good scheduling prevents root rot and drought stress, and daily soil moisture estimates cut the risk of runoff and erosion.

soil-water-165.title: Four benchmarks from soaked to bone-dry
soil-water-165.text: Soil scientists routinely measure four reference water contents, each tied to a suction. Saturated water content, θs, sits at 0 kPa and is typically 0.2–0.5 by volume, equivalent to effective porosity. Field capacity, θfc, sits at −33 kPa and is typically 0.1–0.35, the moisture 2–3 days after rain or irrigation. Permanent wilting point, θpwp, sits at −1500 kPa and is typically 0.01–0.25, the lowest moisture at which a plant wilts. Residual water content, θr, is the water left at very high tension, typically 0.001–0.1. Available water content is field capacity minus wilting point. It ranges from 0.1 in gravel to 0.3 in {{ref:soil-class-070}}. Texture moves every benchmark. Average values put sand's wilting point at 3.3% and its field capacity at 9.1% by volume, against 27.2% and 39.6% for clay. Clay holds far more water, but much of it stays out of reach. Available water peaks in silt loam at 19.7% by volume, against 5.8% in sand and 12.4% in clay.

soil-water-211.title: Why low spots feed the water table
soil-water-211.text: The same rain can refill an aquifer or not, depending on where it pools. Spread evenly within a soil's field capacity, rain barely drains down. Gathered in low spots, the same volume can exceed field capacity and drain to groundwater. In depression-focused recharge, rain falls fairly evenly over an area but reaches groundwater mainly beneath depressions where runoff gathers. Water tables rise beneath them, and the process can matter greatly in arid regions. Deeper ponding forces water in faster and drives adsorbed contaminants down to the water table. In karst, focused flow can dissolve tunnels down to aquifers, an extreme form of preferential flow that speeds contaminant transport.

soil-water-245.title: Spinning soil to gauge its water
soil-water-245.text: In 1910 soil scientists put field capacity in a centrifuge. The moisture equivalent is the percentage of water a soil retains against a force 1000 times gravity, proposed as a measure of field capacity for fine-textured soils. A saturated sample 1 cm thick is spun at 1000 times gravity for 30 min. Its gravimetric water content afterwards is the moisture equivalent. Briggs and Shantz related it to texture in 1912: moisture equivalent = 0.02 sand + 0.22 silt + 1.05 clay. Soil physics no longer uses the concept, and field capacity has replaced it.

soil-water-236.title: How far to let soil dry before watering
soil-water-236.text: A vegetable crop can spare less of its water than an established tree. Management allowed depletion is the percentage of available soil water that can be used up before plants become stressed. It is often set at 50% for standard crops and 30% for sensitive crops such as vegetables. Stress-tolerant plants such as established trees get 60–70%. Soil moisture sensors can then act as a thermostat, triggering irrigation only when moisture drops below the threshold.

soil-water-235.title: Keeping a checkbook for the water in soil
soil-water-235.text: Some irrigators run their soil like a bank account. The soil water balance method, also called the checkbook method, schedules irrigation by tracking deposits and withdrawals. Rain and irrigation are the deposits. Evapotranspiration, the soil's evaporation plus the plants' transpiration, is the withdrawal. Each day's depletion equals the previous depletion plus crop evapotranspiration, minus rain and irrigation. Crop evapotranspiration is reference evapotranspiration, the loss from a standard grass surface, adjusted by a crop coefficient set out in FAO Paper 56. Coefficients above 1 mark high water users such as corn, and below 1 drought-tolerant plants such as cactus. The method relies on accurate weather data.

soil-water-159.title: Percolation: the slow trickle below the roots
soil-water-159.text: After soil drinks in the rain, gravity keeps pulling. Percolation is the downward drainage of water through a soil after the soil has absorbed it. Water draining through macropores under gravity during rain is called gravitational water. Drainage stops at field capacity, when adhesion and cohesion hold the rest. Once a soil is fully wetted, extra water percolates below the roots. It carries clay, nutrients and contaminants that may pollute groundwater, along with the dark organic material of {{ref:soil-bio-089}}. Magnesium, sulfur and potassium leach most readily, and phosphorus very little. Deep percolation that reaches groundwater is groundwater recharge, and groundwater in turn feeds soil moisture through percolation.

soil-water-248.title: Lysimeters: soil in a can, sometimes on a scale
soil-water-248.text: Edward Lewis Sturtevant built the first lysimeter in the United States in 1875. A lysimeter is a soil-filled container, usually a cylinder, used to study how water and dissolved substances move through soil. It can hold an undisturbed soil monolith or rebuilt layers, carry probes at several depths, and collect the water that drains out through an opening at the bottom. Weighing lysimeters sit on scales, so weight changes give evaporation, transpiration and drainage, and hence actual evapotranspiration. Suction lysimeters draw soil water through a buried porous cup under vacuum. Drainage lysimeters collect water passing through the profile to study leaching.

soil-water-230.title: The vadose zone, between the surface and the water table
soil-water-230.text: Between the land surface and the water table lies ground where air and water share the pores. This is the vadose zone, the unsaturated zone, where water in the pores is below atmospheric pressure. Adhesion and capillary action hold its water, and where the zone lies in soil, that water is soil moisture. It excludes the still-saturated {{ref:soil-water-179}} just above the water table. The zone is absent under lakes and marshes but can be hundreds of metres thick in arid regions. It often controls water's path from the surface to aquifers. So it governs recharge, and whether, where and how fast contaminants reach groundwater. Unlike the aquifers below, it is not a ready source of drinking water. Yet it supplies water and nutrients to the biosphere and is heavily used for crops, building and waste disposal. Flow through it is often described by the {{ref:soil-water-238}}, which rests partly on Darcy's law. Its study spans soil physics and hydrology.

soil-water-179.title: The capillary fringe: groundwater climbing into the soil
soil-water-179.text: Groundwater does not stop at the water table. It climbs. The capillary fringe is the layer just above a water table into which groundwater rises by capillary action to fill the pores. Small, uniform pores can keep soil saturated several feet above the water table, while large pores limit the saturated part to a few inches. Because pore sizes are mixed, this tension-saturated base is shorter than the total capillary rise. Above it, water content falls with height. Definitions differ. Solute-transport workers count only the saturated base, while salinity and vapor-phase workers, and those in {{ref:soil-env-023}}, include the unsaturated part too. The fringe has consequences. Land whose surface lies within the capillary fringe of saline groundwater salinizes rapidly. Where the water table meets soil, it forms a boundary between oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor conditions, and oxygen there feeds microbes that break down dissolved organic compounds.

soil-water-221.title: The tensiometer, a gauge of how hard soil holds its water
soil-water-221.text: A tube, a porous cup and a vacuum gauge can tell a farmer when to water. A tensiometer measures the matric potential, or moisture tension, of water in unsaturated soil. It is a water-filled glass or plastic tube with a porous ceramic cup, topped by a vacuum gauge or by a rubber cap read with a needle instrument. Buried and pumped to a partial vacuum, its water comes to balance with soil water through the cup. As plants and evaporation dry the soil, the vacuum grows; when the soil is rewetted, it falls. The gauge then reads the soil's matric potential. Irrigation managers use it to decide when to water. With a water retention curve, it also tells them how much. {{ref:soil-hist-023}} described its principles, construction and operation early in his career and kept improving the design. ISO 11276:1995 sets out tensiometer methods for pore water pressure in unsaturated and saturated soil.

soil-water-238.title: The Richards equation, a famously hard sum for moving water
soil-water-238.text: {{ref:soil-hist-023}} gave his name to an equation he did not write first. The Richards equation, published by Richards in 1931, describes water movement in unsaturated soils. Lewis Fry Richardson had introduced it nine years earlier, in 1922. It joins conservation of mass with the Darcy–Buckingham law for flow in variably saturated porous media, plus a sink term that is usually root water uptake. Its mixed form has two unknowns, water content and pressure head, linked through the water retention curve. It needs the soil's hydraulic properties, usually five van Genuchten retention parameters plus the saturated hydraulic conductivity. It is a quasilinear partial differential equation, solvable analytically only for particular conditions. Alt and Luckhaus proved that solutions exist and are unique only in 1983. Solving it numerically is among the hardest problems in earth science. Solvers may fail to converge, and rain soaking into dry soil needs grid spacing under one cm near the surface. It is still used widely, because it describes flow in the vadose zone between the atmosphere and the aquifer.

soil-water-206.title: Tracking a wetting front as it sinks
soil-water-206.text: The soil moisture velocity equation gives the speed at which water moves down through unsaturated soil under the combined pull of gravity and capillarity. It reworks Richards' equation so that its unknown is the depth of a wetting front of a given water content as it moves with time. An advection-like term carries flow driven by gravity and capillarity, and a diffusion-like term reflects the front's shape. Dropping the second term still gave over 99% accuracy in cumulative infiltration, checked against exact solutions for idealized soils. Solved by the method of lines, the advection-like term becomes three ordinary differential equations, for infiltrating water, falling slugs and capillary groundwater.

soil-water-239.title: A sturdier way to simulate unsaturated flow
soil-water-239.text: Where Richards solvers can fail, this method is guaranteed to converge. The finite water-content vadose zone flow method is a one-dimensional alternative to solving Richards' equation numerically. It solves the advection-like term of the {{ref:soil-water-206}} as three ordinary differential equations, for infiltrating water, falling slugs and capillary groundwater. Being explicit, it is cheap to solve and mass-conserving, and it handles the sharp wetting fronts that Richards solvers struggle with. It assumes soil homogeneous in layers and omits soil water diffusion, which barely affects flux accuracy. It works with any monotonic retention and conductivity relations, such as Brooks and Corey or van Genuchten–Mualem.

soil-water-213.title: Estimating the recharge no one can measure
soil-water-213.text: No widely applicable method can measure groundwater recharge directly and accurately, so hydrologists estimate it. The difficulty is closing the balance. Evaporation, transpiration and infiltration must first be measured or estimated. Common methods include chloride mass balance, soil physics methods, environmental and isotopic tracers, groundwater-level fluctuations, water balances and river baseflow. Direct physical methods measure the water passing below the root zone, while indirect ones infer recharge from soil physical parameters. Numerical codes such as HYDRUS1D, UNSAT-H and SHAW use climate and soil data and some form of the Richards equation to model flow in the vadose zone.

soil-water-158.title: Fingered flow: water falling in narrow fingers
soil-water-158.text: Water does not always sink through dry soil as an even front. In fingered flow it moves down through unsaturated soil unevenly, in narrow 'gravity fingers'. Soil moisture sources attribute the fingers to surface tension between water particles. The fingering is described as a Saffman–Taylor instability. It arises mostly during drainage and leaves an unstable boundary between saturated and unsaturated soil.

reviews.water-in-soil: Water that enters a field leaves it as surface runoff, as drainage through the soil, or by evaporation and transpiration, and this chapter has followed each route. Infiltration lets water in only while there is room at the surface, hydraulic conductivity and Darcy's law set how fast it moves, and water potential sets the direction, always from higher to lower. What stays is held against gravity, more tightly by fine clay than by coarse sand, and field capacity and the permanent wilting point bracket the share plants can use. Below the roots, percolation and recharge carry water through the vadose zone to the water table, flow the Richards equation describes and solvers struggle with. Drainage design, irrigation scheduling and tools from the drying oven to SMAP turn that physics into decisions about when to drain and when to water.
